title: A song in the forest
told: the history and tradition of Guru Gobind Singh at Machhiwara

hook.say: can i ask you something first? when someone asks how you are on a hard day, what do you usually say?
options: fair enough. this story has a third way. listen.

steps.line: Winter, 1704. After years of war, Guru Gobind Singh had lost his home at Anandpur. His companions were scattered, and two of his sons had died in battle.
steps.label: from Sikh history and tradition

steps.line: He walked alone into the forest of Machhiwara, his feet torn and bare. Tradition says he lay on the cold ground, with a lump of earth for a pillow.

steps.q: Alone, with almost everything gone, he sang. What kind of song do you guess?
o: A lament for his lost sons
A war cry to rally his Sikhs
A love song to God, the Friend
steps.why: Not a lament, and not a battle cry. A love song: “go and tell the beloved Friend how his people are.” It’s in the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs still sing it.

steps.line: And there, tradition says, he sang a hymn Sikhs still sing today: go and tell the beloved Friend how his people are.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: A bed of straw with the Friend, the hymn says, is better than a palace without him.

steps.q: Why would someone who lost so much sing that straw with the Friend beats a palace?
o: Nearness to God outweighed his losses
He wanted people to feel sorry for him
steps.why: The hymn doesn’t pretend the loss away. It says the Friend is still there, even on the ground.

steps.line: At dawn his Sikhs found him, and two Muslim brothers, Ghani Khan and Nabi Khan, helped carry him to safety.
Sikhs call it chardi kala: ever-rising spirits. Not pretending it’s fine. Choosing which way your spirit faces, even when things fall.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Enemy soldiers were searching the roads. How did the two Muslim brothers get the Guru past them?
o: Carried him as a Muslim holy man
Hid him in a cart of hay
Led him by night through the river
steps.why: Tradition says they dressed him in blue and carried him on a litter as the “Pir of Uch,” a Sufi holy man. Sikhs still honor the brothers for the risk they took.

steps.q: Your team loses the final. Which of these sounds most like chardi kala?
steps.why: Chardi kala names the loss and then faces up. Sikhs still grieve; the spirit just doesn’t stay face-down.

say: chardi kala isn’t cheerfulness. cheerfulness depends on how things are going. chardi kala is meant to hold when things fall apart.

sikhs say it comes from trust in hukam, the will of god running through everything. sikhs still grieve and weep. chardi kala keeps the spirit pointing up anyway, like a plant reaching for light in a dark room.

steps.q: The hymn calls God “the beloved Friend.” Why might that word matter on the worst night?
o: You can tell a friend how bad it is
A friend will fix it for you
steps.why: The hymn begins: go and tell the Friend how his people are. He doesn’t hide the straw and the cold; he reports them, the way you would to a friend.

today.say: today, when someone asks how you are, try telling the truth, and then one thing that still lifts you. many sikhs answer with just two words: chardi kala.
options: then rise anyway. i’m with you.
that’s allowed. chardi kala starts with being honest about the weight.
